table.text: In all experiments, participants were presented with scenarios consisting of a brief background story, followed by a conditional expressing a character's thought (regardless of whether this character would be willing to assert it to anyone else).

After reading each story, participants were provided with two tables reporting the frequency distributions of the four possible combinations of the antecedent and consequent, alongside their respective negations, that is: ac, ac, ac, and ac.

Participants were then asked to indicate which table, in their view, best captured the character's knowledge of the situation underlying the conditional. 3The rationale behind this experimental paradigm is to avoid asking participants for explicit judgments about the probability, acceptability, or truth of the conditional presented to them, as such questions might easily be misunderstood or bias responses in favor of one account.

table.text: All participants were recruited on Prolific. Inclusion criteria required participants to be native speakers of English residing in the UK and to have a Prolific approval rate higher than 98%. For each experiment, the required sample size was determined by means of an a priori power analysis conducted through a simulation-based approach implemented in R (Green & MacLeod, 2016; Kumle et al., 2021).

For Experiment 1, the power analysis indicated that a total sample of 360 participants would provide 80% power to detect a small effect of the numerosity manipulation. We collected data from 380 participants, 12 of whom were excluded for failing the attention check. Participants received a compensation of £0.63.

live_data_statements: Specifically, in studies within the suppositional tradition, participants were sometimes asked to make these judgments in gambling-like tasks.

For example, in Politzer et al. (2010), participants were shown small arrays of chips that varied in shape and color and asked to estimate the probability that a conditional referring to a randomly selected chip (e.g., "If the chip is square, then it is black") was true.

In all experiments, participants were presented with scenarios consisting of a brief background story, followed by a conditional expressing a character's thought (regardless of whether this character would be willing to assert it to anyone else).

After reading each story, participants were provided with two tables reporting the frequency distributions of the four possible combinations of the antecedent and consequent, alongside their respective negations, that is: ac, ac, ac, and ac.

Participants were then asked to indicate which table, in their view, best captured the character's knowledge of the situation underlying the conditional. 3The rationale behind this experimental paradigm is to avoid asking participants for explicit judgments about the probability, acceptability, or truth of the conditional presented to them, as such questions might easily be misunderstood or bias responses in favor of one account.
In all experiments, participants provided their judgments on multiple pairs of distributions, allowing us to assess the consistency of their responses.
Specifically, participants were classified as consistent when all their judgments aligned with the same account.

Participants were classified as inconsistent when their responses did not show a clear preference between the two accounts (i.e., when 2 of the 4 responses supported each account in Experiments 1 and 3, or when at least 5 out of 12 responses supported each account in Experiment 2).
All participants were recruited on Prolific.
Inclusion criteria required participants to be native speakers of English residing in the UK and to have a Prolific approval rate higher than 98%.

The final sample therefore comprised 368 participants: 187 in the Low-numerosity condition (97 reported their sex as female and 90 as male in their Prolific profiles; Mage = 46.81, SDage = 14.50) and 181 in the High-numerosity condition (88 reported their sex as female and 92 as male, while this information was marked as expired by Prolific for one participant; Mage = 47.87, SDage = 13.05).

Although the conditionals used in our scenarios contained no negations and participants were presented with conditionals rather than arguments, our labeling manipulation bears some relation to research on the implicit negation effect (e.g., Evans & Handley, 1999; Vance & Oaksford, 2021).

We collected a total of 340 participants, of whom 45 were excluded for having failed at least one attention check, leaving a final sample of 295 participants (157 reported their sex as female and 137 as male in their Prolific profiles, while one participant chose not to disclose this information to Prolific; Mage = 45.15, SDage = 13.03).
Participants were compensated with £1.00.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions defined by the combination of the two between-subjects factors.

The final sample therefore comprised 357 participants: 181 in the Predictive condition (87 reported their sex as female and 93 as male in their Prolific profiles, while one participant chose not to disclose this information to Prolific; Mage = 45.66, SDage = 12.99) and 176 in the Diagnostic condition (71 reported their sex as female and 103 as male in their Prolific profiles; one participant chose not to disclose this information to Prolific, while Prolific marked it as expired for another participant; Mage = 46.33, SDage = 13.85).
Participants were compensated with £0.63.

As described in the Method section of Experiment 1, to minimize potential linguistic misunderstandings of the stimuli, which could have been particularly problematic in a study of this kind, we recruited native speakers of English residing in the UK through Prolific.

We chose this platform because, although online samples cannot generally be regarded as fully representative of the broader population, Prolific's UK participant pool is particularly large and heterogeneous.

Our paradigm was partly inspired by Experiment 2 inEvans et al. info.title: Assessing conditionals: An experimental comparison of suppositional and inferential accounts

text.text: Acknowledgment: We thank Mike Oaksford, David Over, and an anonymous reviewer for their generous and helpful comments on the manuscript.

Although conditionals play a key role in hypothetical thinkingfrom making predictions to evaluating explanationsexisting empirical findings have not yet provided a conclusive answer as to when people consider them acceptable.

Using a new experimental procedure that allows a clear distinction between competing theoretical models, this study shows that reasoning about conditionals is context-sensitive: when the antecedent and consequent of a conditional are arbitrarily linked, people tend to rely on how likely the consequent is given the antecedent, whereas when they are causally linked, people focus on whether the antecedent provides a good reason to expect the consequent.

These findings indicate that no single existing model can fully account for how people evaluate different types of conditionals, and they have practical implications for generating more effective hypotheses across various fields.
A conditional is a sentence that expresses a hypothetical statement and consists of an antecedent (the if-clause) and a consequent (the then-clause, in which the word then is sometimes implicit).
For example, "If it is snowing, (then) it is cold" is a conditional, where "It is snowing" is the antecedent (a) and "It is cold" is the consequent (c).
Conditionals are often formally represented as a→c, and the statements expressed are hypothetical, in that neither a nor c are implied by the conditional.
This means that when one asserts "If it is snowing, it is cold," they are not asserting that "It is snowing" or that "It is cold".
What one asserts is that a certain relation holds between "It is snowing" and "It is cold."
Conditional statements play a central role in human reasoning, as they occur in a wide variety of inferences directly involved in the construction and transmission of knowledge.
These range from exploring hypotheses to evaluate outcomes that would obtain under alternative assumptions, to anticipating consequences of future actions.
Scientific predictions are also largely structured around hypothetical statements, as in causal laws or in theory testing (e.g., "If copper is heated, it will expand.")
A paradigmatic example is the inference rule modus ponens: from the premises a→c and a, one can infer the conclusion c.
Thus, for example, if we have reasons to believe that "If it is snowing, it is cold", and we observe that "It is snowing", we can safely conclude that "It is cold".
This rule, which logicians regard as fundamental, essentially relies on the properties of conditionals.
The question of what a conditional is, however, has no easy answer.
The meaning of if, unlike that of not or and, for instancerepresented respectively as  and is particularly hard to capture in formal terms.
According to the material interpretation of conditionals adopted in classical propositional logic, a→c is true if and only if it is not the case that a is true and c is false.
This interpretation, however, is widely regarded as inadequate for capturing the ordinary use of conditionals because of its patently counterintuitive consequences.
For example, suppose that Beth is in Spain.
Then, "If Beth is in Paris, she is in Italy" turns out to be true, and so does "If Beth is in Paris, she is in Spain".

More generally, under the material interpretation, the false antecedent principle (according to which a conditional with a false antecedent is always true) and the true consequent principle (according to which a conditional with a true consequent is always true) hold, so that a→c is entailed by a and by c, respectively.
In order to avoid such unpalatable consequences, a variety of alternative interpretations have been explored, giving rise to extensive and intricate discussions (Edgington, 2025).

text.text: The contemporary debate on conditionals encompasses a wide range of proposals that depart from the material interpretation in different ways.
Although most of them have been examined primarily from a logical perspective, some have also attracted the interest of experimental psychologists.
Indeed, each specific model that has been advanced, independently of normative considerations, can be assessed as an empirical hypothesis about the ordinary use of conditionals.
In what follows, we consider the two accounts that have received the most attention within both communities, outlining their formal aspects and the empirical evidence offered in their favor.
The suppositional account is currently one of the most influential approaches to conditionals in philosophy and psychology.
It builds on the Ramsey Test, according to which asserting a→c amounts to claiming that c holds on the supposition that a holds (Ramsey, 1929 (Ramsey, /1990)).

A second version, developed by Stalnaker (1968 Stalnaker ( /1991)), defines a qualitative criterion of truth in modal terms: a conditional a→c is true if and only if c is true in the closest world in which a is true.

In particular, suppositional approaches elude the false-antecedent and the trueconsequent principles, as well as monotonicity (according to which a conditional remains true when its antecedent is strengthened with additional information).
The suppositional view has been widely regarded as normatively compelling and, intuitively, as a descriptively accurate characterization of conditionals.

Among these, a common task consists of asking participants to estimate, on the basis of frequency information corresponding to the four possible conjunctions of the antecedent and the consequent, the probability that a conditional is true or holds, either in a single judgment or across an extended sequence of trials (e.g., Evans et al., 2003; Fugard et al., 2011).

text.text: These studies consistently led to two main results.
First, the material interpretation of conditionals has been found to be largely counterintuitive.

text.text: Taken together, these findings lend support to the idea that the conjunctive interpretation may reflect an incomplete implementation of the evaluative processes underlying the suppositional interpretation of conditionals.
The main alternative to the suppositional account of conditionals is the inferential one.

text.text: Building on Cheng's (1997) power PC theory, van Rooij and Schulz (2019) model conditional acceptability in terms of a normalized version of ΔP, dividing it by 1-P(c|a).

Under the model's standard assumptions, this normalization makes it possible to estimate the power of the cause expressed by the antecedent (a) to produce the effect expressed by the consequent (c), separately from the influence of background causes, thereby addressing an important limitation of ΔP.
Their analysis also extends to diagnostic conditionals (i.e., conditionals in which the antecedent refers to an effect and the consequent to one of its possible causes).

In this case, the same normalized expression is applied in the diagnostic direction of the conditional (i.e., effect→cause), but, crucially, it is now interpreted as the probability that the cause (mentioned in the consequent) produced the effect (mentioned in the antecedent), given the occurrence of that effect.

The third inferential proposal is the Evidential model advocated by Crupi and Iacona (2022a , 2022b , 2025), which is based on the assumption that a→c holds when a is incompatible with c (thus labelled IN hereafter).

text.text: This assumption, known as the Chrysippus Test, can be made precise in two ways: one yields a quantitative criterion of acceptability in probabilistic terms, the other provides a qualitative criterion of truth in modal terms.

Thus, the conditional a→c is intuitively warranted when the degree of incompatibility between 𝑎 and 𝑐 is sufficiently high.
Conversely, it fails to hold when the incompatibility between 𝑎 and 𝑐 is low or entirely absent.

Reverse Ramsey Test, which requires that a holds in the closest worlds in which c holds, because the incompatibility between a and c is meant to be a symmetric relation.

Earlier studies had already examined whether judgments of conditionals are sensitive to covariation between antecedent and consequent, as measured by ΔP.

Disagreement also concerns the implications of the two accounts, including the so-called centering principle (or conjunctive sufficiency), according to which one may infer a→c from a∧c.
Because centering is valid under the suppositional but not the inferential account, several studies have investigated whether people endorse this inference.

Empirical findings are, once again, mixed: some results provide evidence that they do (Cruz et al., 2016), whereas others suggest that endorsement depends on the inferential connection between the antecedent and the consequent, with particularly low endorsement rates for missing-link conditionals (Douven et al., 2026; Krzyżanowska & Douven, 2018).

text.text: As the discussion above makes clear, the use of missing-link conditionals in this debate is both crucial and delicate.

On the one hand, these conditionals have offered to the inferential account one of its most enduring and widely invoked theoretical arguments, as well as some of the clearest empirical evidence in its favor.
On the other hand, they appear anomalous in many ordinary contexts, which complicates the interpretation of participants' experimental responses.
Notably, neither these conditionals nor their apparent anomaly represents a recent discovery.

Conditionals of this kind -also known as Walrus conditionals, after the Walrus in Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem "The Walrus and the Carpenter" (Over & Evans, 2024) -had already been extensively discussed by linguists and philosophers, including proponents of the suppositional account.

text.text: Without pursuing this side debate further, we simply note that, in our view, the empirical comparison between the suppositional and inferential accounts needs to be broadened beyond missing-link conditionals to include ones in which the antecedent-consequent connection is precisely quantified and experimentally manipulated.
As illustrated when reviewing the empirical support for the two accounts, the results of experimental studies have consistently undermined the descriptive adequacy of the material interpretation.
However, the debate over whether the suppositional or the inferential account better captures how individuals interpret conditionals remains far from settled.

This may be due, at least in part, to the fact that empirical research within the two traditions has typically relied on distinct stimuli and methodologies, neither of which is immune to confounds, as discussed in the following section.

The present study provides an empirical test of the descriptive adequacy of the accounts outlined above by refining and extending existing methodologies, thereby strengthening the evidence available to date.
In particular, we propose a novel experimental paradigm designed to minimize the risk that the stimuli or questions may be misunderstood or may bias responses in favor of either account.
Before introducing this paradigm, we briefly discuss what we deem to be the principal limitations of the extant empirical literature.
Although historically important, previous empirical studies vary in several methodological respects, making their findings difficult to interpret and compare.
A first major issue concerns the stimuli, which have typically differed across studies supporting the two accounts.
With a few exceptions, studies in the suppositional tradition have used arbitrary conditionals referring to randomly selected items from specified frequency distributions.

By contrast, studies taken to support the inferential account have more commonly used conditionals with ordinary content, while measuring (either directly or indirectly) participants' perceived strength of the inferential connection between the antecedent and the consequent, rather than experimentally manipulating that strength.

text.text: To complicate matters further, the stimuli presented could also have influenced how participants interpreted these questions.
Specifically, in studies within the suppositional tradition, participants were sometimes asked to make these judgments in gambling-like tasks.

For example, in Politzer et al. (2010), participants were shown small arrays of chips that varied in shape and color and asked to estimate the probability that a conditional referring to a randomly selected chip (e.g., "If the chip is square, then it is black") was true.

By contrast, as Over and Cruz (2023) argue, in studies framed within the inferential account, participants presented with missing-link conditionals may have understood the question as asking not so much about the conditional itself as about whether a meaningful relation exists between its antecedent and consequent and, possibly, how strong that relation is.

text.text: A third major limitation of previous research is its overreliance on correlational approaches.

Participants' ratings of the truth or acceptability of conditionals have typically been correlated with the values relevant to the models under investigation (i.e., the probability of the consequent given the antecedent or the strength of the association between the two).

These values have been derived either from the frequency distributions provided to participants (e.g., Oberauer, Weidenfeld, and Fischer, 2007), elicited from the same participants who evaluated the conditionals (e.g., Douven et al., 2022; Singmann et al., 2014), or obtained from a different group of participants (e.g., Hadjichristidis et al., 2001, Study 1; Skovgaard-Olsen et al., 2016).

text.text: However, because the probability of the consequent given the antecedent tends to be higher when the inference from antecedent to consequent is stronger, correlational methods are ill-suited to empirically distinguishing between the predictions of the two accounts.

In the present work, we propose a novel experimental paradigm, designed to provide a robust discriminative test of the descriptive adequacy of the main accounts of conditionals advanced in the literature, and we implement it in three online experiments conducted via SoSci Survey (https://www.soscisurvey.de/).

text.text: In all experiments, participants were presented with scenarios consisting of a brief background story, followed by a conditional expressing a character's thought (regardless of whether this character would be willing to assert it to anyone else).

The stories ranged from everyday situations involving hobbies, as in Experiments 1 and 2, to more technical contexts, such as industrial or safety supervision, as in Experiment 3 (see Figure 1 for example scenarios and Supplementary Materials for the full set of stimuli).

text.text: Importantly, each story was framed such that the character was intended to be uncertain about the truth of the antecedent and the consequent of the conditional.
The point of this was to prevent participants from disregarding cases in which the antecedent was false or from focusing exclusively on cases in which the consequent was true.

After reading each story, participants were provided with two tables reporting the frequency distributions of the four possible combinations of the antecedent and consequent, alongside their respective negations, that is: ac, ac, ac, and ac.

Participants were then asked to indicate which table, in their view, best captured the character's knowledge of the situation underlying the conditional. 3The rationale behind this experimental paradigm is to avoid asking participants for explicit judgments about the probability, acceptability, or truth of the conditional presented to them, as such questions might easily be misunderstood or bias responses in favor of one account.

Specifically, the probability of each conjunction was a multiple of .05 and less than .5, so as to reduce the difficulty of processing differences between values and to avoid drawing attention to cells containing numbers with more digits, respectively.

In all experiments, participants provided their judgments on multiple pairs of distributions, allowing us to assess the consistency of their responses.
We counterbalanced the left-right position of the distributions most closely aligned with each of the accounts being compared.
For instance, in Experiments 2 and 3, the table aligned with the suppositional account appeared on the left in half of the trials and on the right in the other half.
Position was also counterbalanced within levels of within-subject factors when present in the experimental design (see below for details).
To minimize order effects, the presentation order of the experimental scenarios (i.e., those relevant to our research questions) was randomized for each participant.

After every four experimental scenarios one filler scenario was presented, which comprised one distribution endorsed by all the accounts considered (including CJ) and another incompatible with all of them.
Responses to filler scenarios served as attention checks, as no reasonable assumption would lead participants to select the distribution that violated all the accounts under consideration.
Compared with previous experimental paradigms, ours offers two main advantages.

First, it does not require participants to evaluate conditionals in terms of abstract -and potentially elusive -notions such as truth or acceptability, which may increase variability in task interpretation and introduce noise into the data.

Second, by employing pairs of distributions explicitly designed to disentangle competing interpretations, it elicits judgments that unambiguously favor one account over the other, thereby reducing the amount of non-discriminative data.
As a first step, we excluded participants who failed the attention check in Experiments 1 and 3 or any of the three attention checks in Experiment 2.

Our main analysis consisted of an account-discriminating test, implemented via a logistic mixed-effects model, with the chosen distribution as the dependent variable, such that the intercept captured the overall tendency to select the distribution aligned with one interpretation of the conditional rather than the alternative.

The model included the other manipulated factors and all possible interactions as fixed effects, as well as random intercepts for participants, distribution pairs and, where necessary, scenarios to account for individual differences and stimulus-level variability (see below and the Supplementary Materials for details).
Additionally, we examined whether judgments were consistent within each participant or whether they alternated between the two accounts under comparison.
Specifically, participants were classified as consistent when all their judgments aligned with the same account.

Participants were classified as inconsistent when their responses did not show a clear preference between the two accounts (i.e., when 2 of the 4 responses supported each account in Experiments 1 and 3, or when at least 5 out of 12 responses supported each account in Experiment 2).
Participants who did not meet these criteria were excluded from the analysis, as it was not possible to distinguish a consistent pattern affected by occasional errors from genuine inconsistency.

A binomial test was then used to assess whether the proportion of consistent participants exceeded that of inconsistent participants, while a chi-square test of independence was used to examine whether this proportion differed across experimental conditions.

In Experiment 1, we examined whether individuals' interpretations of conditionals were consistent with the two normatively grounded theoretical accounts (i.e., the suppositional and inferential accounts) by contrasting their shared prediction with that of the conjunctive interpretation.

To this end, we employed arbitrary conditionals, which figured prominently in much of the early empirical literature -including studies that provided some support for the conjunctive interpretation -thereby allowing us to compare our results directly with previous findings.
To increase the generalizability of our results, we manipulated the number of cases in the distributions presented to participants.

For Experiment 1, we developed the following two scenarios: LOW-NUMEROSITY SCENARIO Lara enjoys teaching her dog simple tricks.

The toys in that set come in various shapes and various colors.
One day, while vacuuming under the sofa, the vacuum bumps into something Lara cannot see, and she figures that one of the toys was left under the sofa.
Given this, Lara thinks: "If the toy is a triangle, then it will be yellow."

The majority of participants' judgments were in line with the suppositional and inferential accounts, whereas only a smaller proportion supported the conjunctive interpretation of conditionals.

Importantly, analyses of response patterns revealed a high degree of intra-individual consistency, with most participants exhibiting a clear preference for one interpretation rather than switching across trials.
The effect of total numerosity only approached statistical significance, despite the substantial difference between the two conditions (i.e., an order-of-magnitude difference).
This suggests that, even if total numerosity might affect participants' responses, its impact is relatively limited within the type of experimental paradigm employed here.
In Experiment 2, we contrasted the suppositional and inferential accounts, again using arbitrary conditionals.
In doing so, we manipulated two factors.

The first was the relevance of the antecedent to the consequent, operationalized as the qualitative Bayesian evidential support (Crupi & Tentori, 2016) that the antecedent provides to the consequent: positive/neutral/negative relevance iff P(c|a)>/=/<P(c), respectively.

text.text: We included this factor because, as discussed above, previous work has shown that it may influence participants' alignment with the accounts.
It is important to clarify, however, that the conditionals in the neutralrelevance condition of our experiment are not missing-link conditionals.
Although their antecedents and consequents are probabilistically independent (i.e., P(c|a) = P(c)), the scenarios nevertheless allow for a potential connection between them.
The second factor concerns the labeling of the expressions designating the complements of the antecedent and the consequent in the frequency-distribution tables.

Specifically, for a conditional such as "If the toy is a triangle, it will be yellow," the distributions presented to participants, as in Experiment 1, referred to alternative predicates (i.e., 'circle' and 'blue') or to negations of the original predicates (i.e., 'not triangle' and 'not yellow').

In Experiment 3, we examined whether the results of Experiment 2 extend to causal conditionals -that is, conditionals conveying a diagnostic or predictive dependency between antecedent and consequent.

Although the suppositional and inferential accounts are, in principle, formulated to apply to conditionals independently of their content, this may not fully hold from a psychological point of view, as people may align with one account or the other depending on the type of conditional being evaluated.

In particular, when reasoning about arbitrary conditionals a suppositional interpretation may suffice, but when the conditional expresses a causal relation, individuals may resort to a more restrictive interpretation, which requires an inferential dependency between antecedent and consequent.

Specifically, we further generalized our investigation of causal conditionals by presenting participants with either predictive conditionals, featuring an enabling cause in the antecedent and one of its possible effects in the consequent (e.g., "If the machinery is jammed, then the package will leak"), or diagnostic conditionals, which presented an effect in the antecedent and a potential enabling cause in the consequent (e.g., "If the package is leaking, then the machinery was jammed"). 7  Evans, Handley, Hadjchristidis, et al. text.text: Experiment 1 provides evidence that most individuals go beyond a purely conjunctive interpretation of conditionals and systematically favor normatively motivated interpretations.

Experiments 2 and 3, in turn, pose a symmetrical and unprecedented challenge to the two normative accounts under consideration by showing that participants' interpretations are not constant but, instead, sensitive to the semantic and structural features of the conditional at issue.
Specifically, when the association between antecedent and consequent is arbitrary, judgments reliably align with the predictions of the suppositional account.

By contrast, when the antecedent and consequent plausibly instantiate a causal link, regardless of its predictive or diagnostic direction, participants' judgments are better aligned with the inferential account.

This pattern of results suggests that, for arbitrary conditionals, participants focused only on the first row of the contingency tables, whereas for causal conditionals they attended to the information contained in both rows: namely, to what happened both in the presence and in the absence of the effect in diagnostic conditionals and to what happened both in the presence and in the absence of the cause in predictive conditionals.
8   The obtained findings offer a comprehensive picture to reconcile a literature that has long appeared theoretically and empirically divided.
Prior studies have alternately supported either the suppositional or the inferential account.
We contend that this oscillation reflects not only the methodological limitations discussed above, but also a systematic sensitivity to the type of conditional under investigation.
What appeared to be empirical disagreement can, in our view, be traced to previously unrecognized heterogeneity in the methods and stimuli employed.

Critically, we have identified a dissociation between the suppositional and inferential interpretations within 8 Our task elicited a forced choice between two distributions rather than a quantitative assessment of how much they differed, as we considered the former type of judgment to be more reliable and robust.
However, it is worth clarifying that the absolute differences between the values assigned by the competing accounts to the distributions being compared cannot explain the reported response patterns.

Indeed, in the negative-relevance and irrelevance conditions of Experiment 2, the differences in P(c|a) were smaller than those yielded by the inferentialist models (particularly DM), yet most responses aligned with the suppositional account.

Moreover, the very same pairs of distributions produced opposite predominant response patterns in the positive-relevance condition of Experiment 2 and in Experiment 3. a single, controlled experimental paradigm, thereby neutralizing methodological variability as a potential source of divergence.

By extending our analysis beyond arbitrary or missing-link conditionals and showing that, for causal conditionals, the same interpretation robustly generalizes across both predictive and diagnostic cases, we have not only advanced the existing debate, but also placed it on firmer and more comprehensive empirical grounds, thereby clarifying the explanatory reach of the competing accounts.
Refinements of current models aimed at achieving a more comprehensive characterization of conditionals could proceed in several directions.

In particular, although both suppositional and inferential accounts have been proved to capture aspects of how conditional assessment operates in human cognition under specific circumstances, they require substantive revision and further theoretical development to accommodate the systematic variability observed across different types of conditionals.

A key strategy for the uncompromising suppositionalist seeking to preserve their analysis as the uniquely correct account of the cognitive representation of conditionals could be to accommodate the data favoring inferentialism (i.e., those from Experiment 3) as driven by pragmatic factors. 9 However, this stance is unlikely to succeed: given our experimental procedure, there is no compelling reason to suppose that participants' responses reflect assessments of conversational appropriateness in Experiment 3 but not in Experiment 2.

text.text: Similarly, the uncompromising inferentialist might attempt to defend their position and question the data favoring suppositionalism (i.e., those from Experiment 2), by arguing that the experimental procedures were not sufficiently effective at disentangling the tasks of assessing conditional acceptability from that of estimating the posterior probability of the consequent given the antecedent.

Here again, the complaint would be hard to maintain: there is no compelling reason to think that participants responded as if prompted to translate a conditional sentence into a conditional probability in Experiment 2 but not in Experiment 3.

A straightforward interpretation of our results is a third possibility, which is viable and no less plausible, although perhaps bound to disappoint purists: the suppositional and inferentialist approaches can be combined, much as they coexist in logic (e.g., Crupi & Iacona, 2022b , 2023; Raidl & Rott, 2024).

text.text: On this view, nontruth-functional conditionals do belong as elements of human cognition in more than one form: individuals would have access to both suppositional and inferential representations, recruiting one or the other depending on contextual and semantic cues, such as the presence or absence of credible and robust causal relations.

Participants' preference for inferential distributions as representations of the acceptability of causal but not arbitrary conditionals would reflect sensitivity to the existence and possibly the strength of the causal dependencies involved.

This interpretation is consistent with evidence from Ali et al. (2011) that people do not rely only on the logical and linguistic form of a conditional, but construct a representation that is sensitive to the direction of the underlying causal relation and structurally analogous to a Causal Bayes net (Pearl, 1988 (Pearl, , 2000;; see Oaksford & Chater, 2020a, for the proposal that Causal Bayes nets can provide a cognitive implementation of inferentialism).

Whatever the future trajectory of the theoretical debate on the interpretation of conditionals, our findings carry significant practical implications.
For example, they can inform research in more applied domains, such as explainable artificial intelligence (XAI).

Systems designed to enhance the interpretability of a model's output -whether in decision-support tools, diagnostic systems, or automated reasoning platforms -often generate or evaluate explanations expressed in conditional form (commonly referred to as "rule-based explanations"; Bodria et al., 2023).

text.text: Effective functioning of these systems requires a solid understanding of how humans interpret "if-then" constructions, as well as which factors shape such interpretations.
Our results suggest that these are not uniform, but rather systematically depend on perceived semantic features and causal relations.
Incorporating this sensitivity into AI systems could enhance their alignment with human reasoning patterns, thereby improving both interpretability and user trust.

More broadly, understanding when individuals adopt a suppositional versus an inferential reading may contribute to the design of explanation strategies that are cognitively natural and context-sensitive.

As described in the Method section of Experiment 1, to minimize potential linguistic misunderstandings of the stimuli, which could have been particularly problematic in a study of this kind, we recruited native speakers of English residing in the UK through Prolific.

We chose this platform because, although online samples cannot generally be regarded as fully representative of the broader population, Prolific's UK participant pool is particularly large and heterogeneous.
Importantly, we have no theoretical reason to believe that the phenomenon investigated here, namely the interpretation of conditionals, depends substantially on demographic or cultural factors.
We therefore expect the findings from our three experiments to generalize to a broader population of adults, although this remains to be confirmed empirically.

A potential theoretical limitation of the present work is that we treated the inferential account as a unitary framework, even though, as noted in the Introduction, it encompasses a range of theoretically distinct models.

An important next step would therefore be to compare the extent to which lay intuitions align with the specific predictions of various inferential models, rather than with the inferential approach as a whole.

Moreover, the present work was limited to the investigation of indicative conditionals, with positive atomic formulas as antecedent and consequent, but the methodology we have introduced could be applied to other types of conditionals, including concessives and counterfactuals, in order to assess whether similar patterns of dissociation persist across a broader range of constructions.

Future research could also more systematically examine whether endorsement of the two interpretations scales proportionally with expectations of the strength of association -causal or otherwise -between antecedent and consequent.

In addition, it would be interesting to use the experimental paradigm described in the present study to compare conditionals beyond those considered in our experiments (i.e., arbitrary conditionals and conditionals whose antecedents and consequents are likely to be perceived as directly causally related).

Among these, relevant cases might include causal conditionals in which the antecedent and consequent are only indirectly linked, as well as conditionals expressing habits, personal dispositions, or social norms.

As argued by Oaksford and Chater (2020a), the extent to which the acceptability patterns of these conditionals align with the predictions of various models may depend on the causal structure underlying the relation between the antecedent and the consequent, as well as on the perceived strength of the relevant dependencies.
